entries.title: A low white cell count that may be Duffy-null (neutrophil count)
entries.answer: Many people of African ancestry are Duffy-null, an inherited blood-cell variant that gives a lower neutrophil count (the white cells that fight infection). The main study calls it clinically insignificant. The risk is being misread: a normal count for you can be flagged as low.

entries.title: Acne on dark skin
entries.answer: Acne in dark skin often leaves dark marks that last longer than the spots, so treating acne early matters most. Retinoid creams and benzoyl peroxide are the usual first treatments, and benzoyl peroxide does not bleach skin. Hair oil, cocoa butter and shea butter on spot-prone skin can clog pores.

entries.title: African black soap
entries.answer: Nobody has tested African black soap on acne, eczema or dark marks in people. A dermatologist says it cleans about as well as other soaps, and some people find it drying. Treat it as a cleanser, not a treatment. Whether it helps your skin is untested.

entries.title: Alpha-thalassaemia trait: small red cells that are not low iron
entries.answer: Alpha-thalassaemia trait means you carry one or two missing copies of the genes that make part of haemoglobin. It is common in people of African descent and can show as small, pale red cells and mild anaemia that looks like low iron. Ask what is behind small red cells before you start iron tablets.

entries.title: Anxiety, depression and what helps
entries.answer: Anxiety and depression are common and treatable, and the NHS says to seek help early. In the UK you can refer yourself to NHS talking therapies, including for social anxiety and panic, without seeing a GP. Whether therapies work differently in Black adults is untested in my search, so choose a service you can attend.

entries.title: Apple cider vinegar: weight, blood sugar and safety
entries.answer: Apple cider vinegar may lower blood sugar and weight slightly in short trials, but the trials are small and varied, and one well-known weight trial was retracted. Our search found no trial of apple cider vinegar in Black participants. Dilute it or use it in food, and avoid the tablets: one injured a throat.

entries.title: Ashwagandha: cortisol, mood, skin, hair, heart, kidneys and liver
entries.answer: In short trials ashwagandha lowered cortisol and stress scores, and a review of 14 trials in mental disorders (mostly anxiety) found less anxiety, with depression less certain. We found no human trial for tension headaches, stress acne or gut. It has been linked to liver injury, deaths in people with liver disease, and one kidney-transplant rejection. Ask a pharmacist first.

entries.title: Ashwagandha: stress, sleep, thyroid and liver cautions
entries.answer: Ashwagandha eased stress and helped sleep a little in short trials, but our search found no trial in Black participants. NCCIH says avoid it in pregnancy, while breastfeeding and with thyroid or autoimmune conditions, and rare liver injury is reported. Ask a pharmacist first, and stop if your skin or eyes turn yellow.

entries.title: Autism and ADHD: being missed, delayed or misdiagnosed
entries.answer: A US review of 20 studies found delayed diagnosis and misdiagnosis of autism were the main errors, driven by limited knowledge, insurance, provider bias and assessment tools that may not suit Black and Hispanic families. Recent US prevalence in Black children is no lower than in White children. My search found no equivalent review for ADHD.

entries.title: Babies' and children's hair
entries.answer: Children's hair is best handled the way adults' is: gently, with hair wet and conditioned for detangling. Tight braids and updos are linked to traction alopecia in Black girls; larger braids, fewer extensions and looser styles are advised. Cradle cap is harmless. My search found nothing aimed at adoptive parents, but the same guidance applies.

entries.title: Baby skin care (newborns and infants)
entries.answer: Newborn skin needs very little: plain water baths for the first month, no cleansers or lotions, and leave vernix on. Jaundice and rashes can be harder to see on brown and black skin, so check the whites of the eyes. A large review, mostly in babies at high risk of eczema, found routine moisturiser probably made no difference to eczema.

entries.title: Baobab fruit: blood sugar, iron and vitamin C
entries.answer: Baobab fruit is a traditional African food and a source of vitamin C. Two small trials in healthy adults in Europe found it lowered the blood sugar rise after a sugary or starchy load. A trial in Kenyan schoolchildren found no significant effect on iron or haemoglobin. My search found no trial in people with diabetes.

entries.title: Being believed by doctors, and pain
entries.answer: Research backs your experience. In US studies Black patients were less likely than white patients to be given painkillers, and many white trainee doctors held false beliefs about biological differences that went with lower pain ratings. It is not you. Prepare, describe what the pain stops you doing, and ask for a plan.

entries.title: Black men, depression and getting support
entries.answer: A survey of African American men found that everyday racism and masculine norms both went with more barriers to seeking help, partly through feeling less in control and more depressed. Depression is a health condition and treatable. You can refer yourself to NHS talking therapies, and the CALM helpline is there for men.

entries.title: Black seed oil (Nigella sativa)
entries.answer: A 2025 review of 82 studies of black seed (Nigella sativa) found small improvements in blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol and body fat, and called it a promising add-on. The trials were not in Black people, and I did not read how sure the authors were. It is not a cure, and not a replacement for medicine.

entries.title: Bovine colostrum supplements for immunity and gut health
entries.answer: Bovine colostrum, the first milk from cows, has small, mixed trials in athletes and a few other groups, with little effect on immune markers. Our search found no trial of colostrum in Black participants. It is a cow's milk product, so check first if dairy upsets you, and do not use it to treat an infection.

entries.title: Bowel (colon) cancer screening
entries.answer: In England the NHS posts a home stool test every 2 years from 50 to 74; US guidance starts at 45. Screening works in the general population, and I found no trial of an earlier start for Black adults. Do the test when it arrives, and see a GP about blood in your poo.

entries.title: Braids, cornrows and twists for men and boys
entries.answer: No study has tested braid styles in men or boys. A South African school survey found traction alopecia mostly in girls with relaxed hair, and neck bumps (acne keloidalis nuchae) in boys with frequent haircuts. Dermatologists' advice is the same for everyone: loose braids, hairline left free, rest between styles.

entries.title: Braids, twists and extensions: tension, how long, itch
entries.answer: Braids that hurt are too tight; pain after installation means pull on the scalp. Dermatologists advise taking braids out within about six weeks and extensions within eight, giving your scalp a break, and keeping the hairline loose. Itch can come from build-up or an allergy to synthetic hair or glue. "Protective" has never been tested.

entries.title: Breast cancer, triple-negative disease and screening
entries.answer: In England, Black women did not have a higher breast cancer rate than White women, but short-term survival was worse in national data, and one London hospital saw younger, more aggressive cases. Know your own breasts and see a GP about any change. NHS breast screening starts between 50 and 53, bowel screening at 50.

entries.title: Breathwork and slow breathing
entries.answer: Slow breathing practice lowers stress and blood pressure a little in trials of adults generally. In the few small studies of African American adults the results were mixed, and one found breathing alone did nothing straight away. It is an extra, not a replacement for treatment.

entries.title: Bush teas and herbal remedies (cerasee, bitter leaf) with medicines
entries.answer: Natural does not mean safe with medicine. A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence that bitter melon (cerasee) helps type 2 diabetes. Memorial Sloan Kettering warns it can add to diabetes medicines and reports case reports of serious harm. The UK's NHS says do not mix herbal medicines with certain medicines, and always check with a pharmacist.

entries.title: Caribbean and West African diets and health
entries.answer: No trial has tested a traditional Caribbean or West African diet for blood pressure or diabetes, so nobody can say whether it is better or worse. What is tested is the pattern: more fruit and vegetables, less salt and saturated fat lowered blood pressure in a mostly Black US trial. Judge your own plate on that pattern.

entries.title: CCCA: scarring hair loss at the crown
entries.answer: CCCA is a scarring hair loss that starts as a thin patch at the crown and spreads outwards. It mostly affects women of African descent and men can have it. Scarred follicles do not regrow, so treatment aims to stop it spreading. The earlier a dermatologist sees it, the more hair is kept.

entries.title: Chebe powder: length retention, growth claims and safety
entries.answer: Chebe is a traditional herbal hair powder, mixed with oil or butter and coated on the lengths. My search found no study of it on hair or in people. A doctor quoted by PureWow says it does not grow hair. Any benefit is untested, so patch test first and avoid heavy coating on thin strands.

entries.title: Chemical relaxers and hair straighteners
entries.answer: Studies disagree on whether relaxers raise cancer risk, and none can prove cause. In the large Black women's cohort, heavy use showed no clear rise in uterine cancer overall but a higher risk after the menopause; breast cancer results were largely null. Relaxed hair under tight styles carried the highest risk of hair loss.

entries.title: Childhood trauma and where to start
entries.answer: Hard things in childhood, such as abuse, neglect or violence at home, raise the chance of anxiety, depression and PTSD later. What happened was not your fault. Trauma-focused therapies help, and you can start with a GP or, in England, a self-referral to NHS talking therapies. You do not have to tell the whole story at once.

entries.title: Choosing a stylist, braider or loctician
entries.answer: No study shows that a stylist's training or specialism gives better hair or scalp outcomes. In one small US survey, most Black cosmetologists had never heard of two scarring hair-loss conditions. Book a consultation or a simple wash first, watch how they handle your hair, and tell them when a style hurts.

entries.title: Cod liver oil: vitamin D, vitamin A and colds
entries.answer: Cod liver oil is a source of vitamin D, which the UK's NHS says people with dark skin should consider taking all year. A large trial in Norwegian adults found it did not prevent covid or other chest infections. It is also high in vitamin A, so too much, or liver products in pregnancy, can do harm.

entries.title: Collagen for hair, nails and joints
entries.answer: Collagen may ease knee osteoarthritis pain a little in pooled trials, though those trials disagreed with each other. For hair and nails we found a few small trials of branded products with mixed results. Our search found no trial in Black participants. It is not a medicine: for hair loss or sore joints, get the cause checked first.

entries.title: Collagen supplements for skin and joints
entries.answer: Collagen supplements may add a little skin moisture in trials, but the best-quality trials and the ones not paid for by the industry found no clear skin effect. Our search found no trial in Black participants or on dark skin. Check labels for fish if you are allergic, and treat promised skin changes as unproven.

entries.title: Colonoscopy: when to start and how often
entries.answer: In the US, screening starts at 45 and a colonoscopy every 10 years is one way to do it. In England, the NHS starts at 50 with a home stool test every 2 years; a colonoscopy follows a positive result. Our search found no study showing Black adults should start before 45. Symptoms, polyps or family history change timing.

entries.title: Colouring and bleaching afro-textured hair
entries.answer: Bleaching and dyeing damage the hair surface whatever the curl, in lab tests on hair samples; no study has tested a colour or bleach routine in people with coiled hair. Dermatologists advise 2 weeks after a relaxer, and the UK's NHS a strand test at least 48 hours before dyeing, because dye can cause allergy.

entries.title: Colourism, skin tone and mental health
entries.answer: In US surveys of Black adults, experiencing colourism within the community went with higher odds of a psychiatric disorder, and among older adults the link between discrimination and distress was stronger in darker-skinned people. These are associations, not proof of cause. No trial has tested a way to cope with it, so use ordinary mental health support.

entries.title: Coping with anxiety day to day
entries.answer: Anxiety is common and treatable. The UK's NHS and the US's NIMH both say regular exercise, enough sleep, less caffeine, calming breathing and talking to someone you trust can help. Two small pilots in Black adults found mindfulness feasible. Nothing we found tests the popular 3-3-3 rule. If it stops you living normally, get help.

entries.title: Creatine supplements: strength, kidneys and your kidney test
entries.answer: Creatine helps strength gains when you train with weights, in trials of mostly young men, and reviews found no kidney harm in healthy adults. Our search found no creatine trial in Black participants. It raises the creatinine kidney marker, so tell anyone reading your kidney tests, and check with a doctor first if you have kidney problems.

entries.title: Dark circles under the eyes
entries.answer: Dark circles under the eyes can come from pigment, thin skin showing blood vessels, or lost volume, and the cause decides the treatment. A systematic review found many treatments help some people, from creams and peels to fillers, but the studies are weak and not specific to Black skin. Daily sunscreen is a sensible start.

entries.title: Dark marks after acne (post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation)
entries.answer: Dark marks after spots are common in dark skin and slow to fade. One trial in Black adults found a prescription retinoid cream lightened them, though many users were irritated. Treating spots early and wearing sunscreen are the main advice. Bleaching products can do real harm.

entries.title: Dark or swollen lips
entries.answer: Dark lips are often a harmless variation in pigment. Smoking and an allergy to a lip product can also darken lips, and a single new dark spot needs a clinician to look at it. Sudden lip swelling can be an allergic reaction, so call emergency services (999 in the UK) if your throat tightens or breathing is hard.

entries.title: Dark velvety patches on the neck and folds (acanthosis nigricans)
entries.answer: Dark, thick, velvety patches in the neck, armpits or groin are called acanthosis nigricans. They are often a sign of insulin resistance, and the UK's NHS says to have them checked by a doctor. Scrubbing and lightening creams do not treat the cause. They fade over time once the cause is treated.

entries.title: Does diet cause acne? Sugar, dairy and foods linked to spots
entries.answer: No diet is proven to treat acne, and the British Association of Dermatologists says a healthy, balanced diet is all it advises. Some studies link sugary, refined foods and dairy to more spots. A 12-week trial in 43 Australian men found a low-glycaemic diet reduced spots. In Nigerian teenagers, milk, fried beef and cake were linked to more acne.

entries.title: Dry, itchy, flaky scalp and dandruff
entries.answer: Flaking and itch are often dandruff or seborrhoeic dermatitis, which is a skin reaction, not simple dryness. An anti-dandruff shampoo, such as ketoconazole, coal tar or salicylic acid, is the UK's NHS first step; ketoconazole beat placebo in trials of mixed people (low-quality evidence). Lice can affect any hair; find a live louse before treating.

entries.title: Eczema on dark skin (atopic eczema, including babies)
entries.answer: Eczema on dark skin often looks grey, purple, brown or darker, not red, with very dry, thickened or bumpy skin. Moisturising at least twice a day, washing with emollient instead of soap, and a pharmacist or doctor for steroid creams are the standard care. A trial of a prescription cream included many Black participants.

entries.title: Fasting in Ramadan with diabetes or sickle cell
entries.answer: With diabetes, fasting in Ramadan can cause low blood sugar and dehydration, and the evidence on sickle cell disease is small and mixed. None of the studies was of Black Muslims as a group. Diabetes UK says do not fast if your diabetes is poorly controlled. Agree a plan with your diabetes or sickle cell team before Ramadan.

entries.title: Fibroids, food and supplements
entries.answer: No food has been shown to shrink fibroids. In Black women, a high glycaemic index diet was only weakly linked to fibroid risk. Five trials of vitamin D in other populations found smaller fibroids, and one tiny trial of green tea extract found the same; both need larger trials. See a doctor for heavy bleeding.

entries.title: Fibroids: symptoms, treatment and pregnancy
entries.answer: Fibroids are non-cancerous growths in or around the womb, and by 50 more than eight in ten Black women in one US study had them. Many have no symptoms and need no treatment. If heavy or painful periods, pressure or fertility worries affect your life, see a GP: there are medicines, and several procedures other than hysterectomy.

entries.title: Finding a Black therapist or one who understands being Black
entries.answer: Directories in the UK and US list Black or culturally aware therapists. Research finds people moderately strongly prefer a therapist of their own background, but matching made almost no difference to how well treatment worked on average. The gaps were widest in studies of African American clients. A good fit matters more than the label alone.

entries.title: Finding a dermatologist who knows dark skin
entries.answer: Dark skin is under-represented in textbooks, and in one test dermatologists and AI both did worse on dark-skin photos, so it is fair to ask a clinician about their experience. In the UK a GP referral is the route; the BAD hub shows how common conditions look on black and brown skin.

entries.title: Finding a stylist, trichologist or dermatologist who knows afro hair
entries.answer: A stylist or loctician is the right person for styling and a trichologist or dermatologist for hair loss. In the UK a GP can refer you to a dermatologist; trichologists are not medically qualified, so check that they are registered and have experience with afro-textured hair. Ask directly what share of their patients have hair like yours.

entries.title: G6PD deficiency: who carries it and what to avoid
entries.answer: G6PD deficiency is an inherited enzyme shortage, common in people with African, Mediterranean and Asian ancestry. Most carriers feel well. Red blood cells break down only when something stresses them, such as an infection, fava beans or certain medicines. A simple blood test finds it, so ask for one before malaria treatment with primaquine.

entries.title: Getting a child mental health support
entries.answer: In English child mental health services, children from Black and other minority backgrounds were more often referred through school or social care than through a doctor. The UK's NHS has guides for parents and information on services for young people. Childline offers free help to anyone under 19.

entries.title: Glaucoma and eye tests
entries.answer: Glaucoma is more common in Black populations at every age, and often has no symptoms until sight is lost. A pooled analysis found the highest prevalence in Black populations at all ages. Have an eye test at least every two years, and ask whether you qualify for a free NHS (UK) test, for example if a close relative has glaucoma.

entries.title: Going natural: transitioning from a relaxer and the big chop
entries.answer: There is no study of the big chop or of how to grow out a relaxer, so none of this is tested. Dermatology guidance on relaxers is clear: never relax hair that is already relaxed, and avoid tight styles. The advice about the weak join between the two textures and trimming comes from hair media, not research.

entries.title: Haemoglobin and white cell ranges on your blood test
entries.answer: Blood test ranges were mostly built from white populations. In large studies, Black adults have lower average haemoglobin and white cell counts, partly from inherited traits such as alpha-thalassaemia and Duffy-null, and partly from low iron. A result outside the range can still be real, so ask what is behind it.

entries.title: Hair breakage, growth and keeping length
entries.answer: Tightly coiled hair does grow, but it breaks more easily when combed or handled, so the length you keep depends on breakage. Company studies measure slower growth in African hair, but nobody has tested how to keep length. Gentle detangling is the best-supported step. No product is shown to repair a strand.

entries.title: Hair growth oils and supplements: castor, rosemary, black seed, biotin
entries.answer: Castor oil alone and black seed oil have not been tested for hair growth in people in my search. Rosemary oil matched 2% minoxidil in one trial of 100 people with pattern baldness, none chosen for afro hair. Biotin helps only if you are deficient, and it can distort blood tests. Growth supplements are mostly brand-run trials in other groups.

entries.title: Hair porosity and moisture
entries.answer: The glass-of-water float test, and routines chosen by "low, normal or high porosity", have never been tested in people. Porosity is real in the lab, but nobody has shown that choosing products by it helps. The lab does show tightly coiled hair breaks easily under rough grooming, so gentle handling is the safest advice.

entries.title: Hair shedding after pregnancy, illness or stress
entries.answer: A sudden all-over shed, usually three months after a trigger such as childbirth, illness, stress or crash dieting, is called telogen effluvium. It usually gets better on its own within months. But thinning at the crown, part or hairline can be a different condition, and some women have both. Ask a doctor to check iron and thyroid if it persists.

entries.title: Hair transplants in afro-textured hair
entries.answer: Transplants can be done on tightly curled hair, but the evidence is a small case series and a review, with no outcome data in Black men. Curl makes extraction harder, so the surgeon's tools and experience matter. Scarring hair loss such as CCCA must be ruled out first.

entries.title: Hair types 4a, 4b, 4c: what typing tells you
entries.answer: The 4a, 4b and 4c letters sort curl by eye and were not checked against measured hair. They do not predict which product or routine will work. Describe your hair instead by how tight the curl is, how wide the strand is and how dense it is. Why texture changes after pregnancy or with age is untested.

entries.title: Head lice in afro-textured hair and locs
entries.answer: Anyone with hair can get head lice. Old school surveys found fewer cases in children with African hair, but they conflict and none looked at locs. Treatment in locs and braids is untested. The UK's NHS advises wet combing or a medicated lotion and does not mention locs; a nit comb may not pass through tight coils.

entries.title: Heat, silk press, keratin treatments and colour
entries.answer: Heat damage on afro hair has not been measured in people. Dermatologists advise a heat protectant, the lowest setting that works and no more than one press a week. One small survey links frequent heat to hairline loss. Keratin smoothing products can release formaldehyde; bleaching and dyeing damage the hair surface whatever your curl.

entries.title: Heat, sweating and hydration
entries.answer: I found no study that shows Black people tolerate heat better or sweat differently. What exists is old, small, and in men who were already acclimatised. Heat risk follows fitness, acclimatisation, body size and exposure. Follow the UK's NHS heat advice, and take extra care if you or your child has sickle cell disease or trait.

entries.title: Heavy periods by life stage and cause
entries.answer: The NHS (UK) says heavy periods can be normal after pregnancy or approaching menopause; ACOG (US) says heavy bleeding is not normal. Either way, get it checked if bleeding disrupts your life or you feel tired or breathless. In a small US study, about two thirds of 44 African American women had iron deficiency; about half reported heavy periods.

entries.title: Hibiscus (sorrel, zobo, bissap) and blood pressure
entries.answer: Hibiscus tea lowered blood pressure a little in several trials, including one in Nigerian adults. A stricter review found too little reliable evidence, so the effect is contested. It is a reasonable drink, not a replacement for blood-pressure medicine.

entries.title: High blood pressure in Black adults
entries.answer: The line for high blood pressure is the same for every adult. In England, blood pressure in people of African-Caribbean origin overtakes White people's at around 30 to 40 (about 28 for men's systolic pressure), so being young and fit does not rule it out. Get it checked. If you need tablets, NICE names a different first choice for you.

entries.title: HIV prevention, testing and PrEP
entries.answer: PrEP is a medicine you take before a possible exposure to HIV, and it is highly effective when taken as prescribed. It comes as tablets, injections or a vaginal ring depending on where you live. Get an HIV test first and then regularly. HIV treatment is effective, so knowing your status is a good thing.

entries.title: How skin conditions look on dark skin (redness, rashes, rosacea, sunburn)
entries.answer: Redness on dark skin can look pink, purple, brown, grey or just a subtle darkening, so it is easy to miss. Eczema, rosacea and sunburn all happen on dark skin and are often under-diagnosed. Compare the affected area with your unaffected skin, and tell your doctor what changed.

entries.title: How some medicines work differently by gene
entries.answer: Genes change how fast your body breaks down some medicines. The variable is the gene, and some versions are more common in people of African ancestry. Examples are ACE inhibitor tablets, which cause face or throat swelling more often in Black patients, and warfarin, whose dose needs gene variants the first formulas missed.

entries.title: Ice baths and cold exposure
entries.answer: Ice baths eased muscle soreness after exercise in small, low-quality trials that did not report ethnicity. No trial has tested them in people of African descent, and cold injury was far more common in African American soldiers in one British army clinic. Cold shock is a real risk.

entries.title: Intermittent fasting for weight and health
entries.answer: Intermittent fasting lost weight in trials, about the same as ordinary calorie cutting, and one small pilot of Black adults in churches found it workable. Avoid it if you have had an eating disorder or are pregnant or breastfeeding, and plan it with your care team if you have diabetes. Religious fasting has its own guidance.

entries.title: Intermittent fasting for women, older adults, teenagers and people with heart or thyroid conditions
entries.answer: Intermittent fasting is not one answer for everyone. In trials of women with overweight, it lowered BMI and fasting blood sugar a little. Australia's official health service says it is not recommended for children, teenagers or older adults. Nothing we found tests it in Black women by life stage, or with thyroid or heart disease. Talk to your doctor first.

entries.title: Iron, heavy periods and fibroids
entries.answer: Fibroids are very common in Black women and start earlier than in White women. Heavy periods can drain iron, and in a small US pilot most African American women had low iron. Do not treat tiredness or heavy bleeding yourself: ask a doctor for a blood test.

entries.title: Keloids and piercings
entries.answer: Keloids run in families and are much more common in people of African ancestry. Nobody has tested whether avoiding piercings prevents them, but the UK's NHS advises prone people to avoid piercings and tattoos. If one forms, early treatment is the advice.

entries.title: Kidney disease, the APOL1 gene and the eGFR race adjustment
entries.answer: Two variants of the APOL1 gene, common on African chromosomes, raise the risk of some kidney diseases in African Americans. Early kidney disease usually has no symptoms. UK guidance no longer adjusts the kidney blood test (eGFR) for Black ethnicity. If you have high blood pressure or diabetes, ask about regular kidney checks.

entries.title: Kola nut: caffeine, the heart and health claims
entries.answer: Kola nut is a traditional stimulant chewed and shared across West Africa. My search found no human study of what it does to health. Its main active ingredient is caffeine, so normal caffeine cautions apply, including a daily limit in pregnancy. Lab and animal findings on the heart and on nitrosamines are untested in people.

entries.title: Lactose intolerance and dairy
entries.answer: Not every Black person is lactose intolerant, and there is no race rule. Whether you keep making lactase, the enzyme that digests milk sugar, depends on your genes, and several separate gene variants that keep it switched on are known in East African groups. Symptoms after dairy are checked with a food trial or a breath test.

entries.title: Laser hair removal on dark skin
entries.answer: Laser hair removal can work in medium to dark skin, but the laser also targets skin pigment, so burns and dark or pale marks are more likely. A review of trials found Nd:YAG lasers gave fewer dark marks than light-based IPL devices. Choose an experienced clinician and ask which laser they use.

entries.title: Lion's mane and reishi mushroom supplements
entries.answer: Lion's mane and reishi have only small trials behind them, mostly low quality, in older Japanese adults with memory loss, healthy adults, and cancer patients on treatment. Our search found no trial of these mushrooms in Black participants. Treat claims for memory or immunity as untested for you, and tell your doctor or pharmacist you take them.

entries.title: LOC and LCO: layering liquid, oil and cream
entries.answer: Nobody has tested layering liquid, oil and cream on people, so there is no proof that LOC or LCO beats one product or that either order is better. Dermatologists say to moisturise regularly between washes. Lab work shows African hair holds lipids differently, but that does not test a routine.

entries.title: Locs: starting, washing and keeping them healthy
entries.answer: No study has tested how often to wash or retwist locs. The British Association of Dermatologists warns that very long locs and tight twisting at the roots strain the scalp and raise the risk of traction alopecia, and that locs must dry fully to avoid mould. Loc-care sites suggest washing every week to month, depending on how much you sweat.

entries.title: Low haemoglobin, low or high white cells: causes, thresholds and pregnancy
entries.answer: Low haemoglobin is called anaemia. Iron shortage is the commonest cause; others include blood loss, infection, other vitamin shortages and inherited traits. White cell counts shift with infection, medicines and pregnancy. Lab ranges vary, and a Duffy-null result can sit below the usual neutrophil line without being a disease. Your doctor needs the cause, not just the number.

entries.title: Lung function tests and race correction in spirometry
entries.answer: A spirometry test measures how much air you can blow out in one breath. For years the machine compared Black patients with a lower predicted normal than white patients, which can hide lung disease. Guidelines now recommend one race-neutral set of equations. The test is still useful, and your symptoms matter as much as the number.

entries.title: Lupus: symptoms, risk and getting diagnosed early
entries.answer: Lupus is a long-term autoimmune condition that causes joint pain, rashes and deep tiredness. It is more common in women of African and Caribbean background and can affect the kidneys, so finding it early matters. See a GP if symptoms keep coming back. Sun protection and regular check-ups help once diagnosed.

entries.title: Magnesium supplements for sleep and cramps
entries.answer: Magnesium tablets did not clearly prevent leg cramps in older adults, and for sleep three small, low-quality trials in older adults hint at falling asleep a little faster. Our search found no supplement trial in Black participants. Up to four hundred milligrams a day from supplements is unlikely to harm; more can cause diarrhoea.

entries.title: Meditation
entries.answer: Meditation is among the better-tested practices here. A trial in Black adults with heart disease found fewer deaths, heart attacks and strokes with Transcendental Meditation. A large review found benefit for anxiety, depression and pain, but no better than other treatments. It adds to medical care and does not replace it.

entries.title: Melasma
entries.answer: Melasma is brown or greyish patches on the face, linked to sun, pregnancy and hormonal medicines. There is no cure, but sun protection plus a prescribed cream usually helps, and it can return. The best-studied cream is hydroquinone, in trials that were not specifically in Black people, so see a dermatologist before lightening products.

entries.title: Melatonin for sleep: what it does, dose and rules by country
entries.answer: Melatonin may help you fall asleep a little faster for some people, but reviews disagree, and it did not clearly help adults with long-term insomnia. In Black patients it has been tested only for night blood pressure, with no effect. Rules differ by country: prescription-only in the UK, a supplement in the US. Labels often miss the real dose.

entries.title: Men's afro hair: waves, fades, durags and the nape
entries.answer: No study has tested a waves routine or durags for scalp or hair health. Barber guides say brush, moisturise and wear a satin durag; that is untested. The part with a medical record is the nape: bumps from very close cuts or shaving there can be acne keloidalis nuchae, a scarring condition in men of African descent.

entries.title: Moisturising and 'ashy' skin
entries.answer: Ashiness is dry skin showing as a grey-white look on dark skin. In a small trial of women with darker skin types, a moisturising body wash or mild bar used regularly reduced dryness and ashiness, with no untreated comparison group. Whether Black skin is naturally drier is contested.

entries.title: Moringa: blood sugar, blood pressure and general health
entries.answer: Moringa leaf is a nutritious food, but a 2025 review of nine trials found no consistent benefit for blood sugar, weight or cholesterol, and rated the evidence very low certainty. A small trial in Nigerian adults with type 2 diabetes found no difference in blood sugar after two weeks. Do not swap it for medicine.

entries.title: Normal blood pressure by age and sex, and for children
entries.answer: There is one blood pressure line for all adults, not a different normal by age or sex. In the UK, a clinic reading of 140/90 or higher is high; in the US, under 120/80 counts as normal and 130/80 starts stage 1. Age changes the treatment target, not the diagnosis. Children are judged against paediatric tables.

entries.title: PCOS, endometriosis and heavy periods
entries.answer: Heavy or painful periods are not something you have to accept. Fibroids are clearly more common in Black women. Endometriosis was the same or lower in US studies, though the data are unclear, and PCOS (now PMOS on the NHS) looked milder in one US trial cohort. See a GP with notes of your symptoms.

entries.title: Plantain, yam and cassava: blood sugar and safety
entries.answer: In glucose tests, cassava, pounded yam and several West African staples raised blood sugar quickly, while breadfruit, white yam, eddoes and tannia were in the middle. Plantain results vary by ripeness and cooking. Cassava must be fully processed, since undercooked bitter cassava has caused paralysis. No trial shows that swapping staples prevents diabetes.

entries.title: Pregnancy risk and safe maternity care for Black women
entries.answer: In England, Black women are nearly three times as likely to die during pregnancy or within six weeks of it as White women, in the latest national report. A confidential enquiry found bias in the care some received. Go to every antenatal check, learn the warning signs, and call your maternity unit straight away if one appears.

entries.title: Probiotics and gut health
entries.answer: Probiotics reduced diarrhoea caused by antibiotics in trials, and the UK's NHS says they may ease some IBS symptoms, but evidence for most other claims is thin. Our search found one small safety pilot in Black women, for vaginal health, and no gut trial in Black participants. Avoid them if your immune system is weak unless your doctor agrees.

entries.title: Prostate cancer risk and PSA testing
entries.answer: In England, about one in four Black men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer in their lifetime, against about one in eight White men. There is no routine NHS PSA screening for Black men: the UK National Screening Committee advised against it in 2026. You can still ask your GP about a PSA test and weigh the risks and benefits.

entries.title: Protecting your edges and hairline
entries.answer: Edges thin mainly from pulling: tight styles, glue on the hairline and frequent heat are linked to hairline loss. Caught early and with the pulling stopped, hair can regrow within months; long-standing loss can be permanent. Edge products have not been tested. If your edges are thinning, see a doctor early.

entries.title: Psychosis, sectioning and misdiagnosis in the UK
entries.answer: In England, Black people are detained under the Mental Health Act more often than any other group, and a large review found Black Caribbean and Black African patients were far more likely to be compulsorily admitted. Why is not settled. If you are detained, you can appeal, ask for an advocate and complain.

entries.title: Pulse oximeters and dark skin
entries.answer: Pulse oximeters shine light through the skin, and melanin changes how that light behaves. In a large US hospital study, readings that looked safe hid low blood oxygen more often in Black patients. A UK review says the devices are valuable and should not be dropped, but need to be tested on darker skin tones.

entries.title: Racism, racial stress and mental health
entries.answer: Many studies find that people who report experiencing racism have worse mental health, including more depression, anxiety and stress. This shows a link, not proof of cause, but it means the strain is real and not a personal failing. Talking therapies, including for trauma, are available.

entries.title: Rashes on dark skin: what to look for
entries.answer: On brown and black skin, the redness of a rash can be harder to see, so it may look darker, or show mainly as raised, rough or itchy skin. Check texture, not just colour. For a fever with a rash, press a clear glass on it and check palms and soles: spots that do not fade are an emergency.

entries.title: Receding hairline and hair transplants in Black men
entries.answer: Receding hairlines have several causes: inherited pattern baldness, pulling from tight styles, or scarring conditions such as CCCA, which men can get. Minoxidil and finasteride are the standard treatments but I found no trial in Black men. Transplants can be done on curly hair but need a specialist and are private in the UK.

entries.title: Relaxer, texturiser, perm and keratin: what is the difference
entries.answer: A relaxer straightens, a texturiser loosens curl by being left on for less time, and a perm adds curl. Stylists say relaxer and texturiser use the same kind of chemical. No study compares their safety. Keratin smoothing products are applied with blow-drying and flat-ironing, and some release formaldehyde.

entries.title: Salt and blood pressure
entries.answer: Cutting salt lowers blood pressure in Black and non-Black adults alike, and the DASH eating pattern did too in a large US feeding trial that was mostly Black. Salt matters, but a special inherited salt gene is not established, and historians dispute the slavery-era theory behind it. Aim for no more than 6g a day, like every adult.

entries.title: Sarcoidosis: symptoms, risk and follow-up
entries.answer: Sarcoidosis is a rare condition where small patches of swollen tissue form, most often in the lungs, skin and lymph nodes. In studies it is more common, and in some studies more severe, in Black adults. Many cases settle without treatment, but a lasting cough, breathlessness or sore red eyes need a doctor.

entries.title: Sauna and heat bathing: heart health, recovery and risks
entries.answer: Frequent sauna use went with fewer heart deaths in Finnish men, a link that falls short of proof, and Black participants were tested only in one tiny heat study. Keep sessions to fifteen or twenty minutes, skip alcohol, watch for dehydration, and ask a doctor first if you have heart or blood pressure problems or sickle cell trait.

entries.title: Scalp oiling and greasing
entries.answer: Nobody has tested scalp oiling or greasing for hair growth or scalp health in a trial. In the lab, coconut oil protected hair strands from protein loss, which is about the strand, not the scalp. Whether the routine does what tradition says is untested.

entries.title: Sea moss (Irish moss): health claims, iodine and heavy metals
entries.answer: My search found no human study showing sea moss improves health. It contains iodine, which in excess can upset the thyroid, and seaweed can carry heavy metals such as arsenic and cadmium. Avoid it while breastfeeding, and ask your doctor first if you have a thyroid condition.

entries.title: Shaving and razor bumps (pseudofolliculitis barbae)
entries.answer: Razor bumps happen when tightly curled hair grows back into the skin after shaving. In one trial of Black men, shaving two or three times a week gave fewer ingrown hairs than daily shaving, but bump counts and doctor-rated severity did not differ. Small trials found hair-removal creams gave fewer bumps but more irritation.

entries.title: Shea butter
entries.answer: Shea butter has been used on skin and hair in West Africa for generations, but no controlled trial has tested plain shea butter on skin. The studies that exist used shea-containing creams or compounds taken from shea, which are not the same thing. Whether it beats other moisturisers is untested.

entries.title: Sickle cell disease, trait and pregnancy
entries.answer: Sickle cell disease is a lifelong inherited blood condition; trait means you carry one copy of the gene and do not have the disease and cannot develop it. If both parents carry it, a child can have the disease. In pregnancy, carriers had low risks in a review, but more anaemia and bacteria in the urine, so ask about checks.

entries.title: Sickle cell disease: what it is, treatment and newborn screening
entries.answer: Sickle cell disease is inherited: you need the gene from both parents. One copy is trait, not the disease. A blood test tells you. Newborn screening is offered in the UK (NHS) and all US states, not yet universally in sub-Saharan Africa. Care helps manage it; in the US, life expectancy is about 20 years shorter.

entries.title: Sickle cell trait and hard exercise
entries.answer: Sickle cell trait is one copy of the sickle gene, not sickle cell disease. It raises the risk of serious muscle breakdown in very hard exercise. A soldiers' study found no clear difference in deaths (a wide margin of error); a US college football study found far more exertional deaths. Know your status and train with care.

entries.title: Skin ageing in dark skin
entries.answer: Reviews say darker skin tends to show lines and sun damage later, helped by more melanin and a thicker, more compact dermis. It is, though, more prone to uneven colour and dark spots. These reviews cover several groups, not only Black people. Daily sunscreen and not smoking are the best-supported habits.

entries.title: Skin cancer and moles on dark skin
entries.answer: Skin cancer is much rarer in Black people, but it can happen, and when melanoma does, outcomes are worse. It is often on palms, soles or under nails rather than sun-exposed skin. Check your whole skin, including those places, and have any new, changing or non-healing mark looked at early.

entries.title: Skin lightening and bleaching creams
entries.answer: Many skin lightening creams contain mercury, strong steroids or high-strength hydroquinone, and reported cases show serious skin and kidney harm. Lightening the whole body is not supported as safe. If dark patches or marks are the worry, there are treatments that target them and are tested in dark skin.

entries.title: Skincare order and layering
entries.answer: No study or guidance we opened sets one correct order for a whole routine. Dermatology guidance gives the steps: wash gently, moisturise, and use sunscreen by day. In a test in 25 volunteers, UV reflectance did not differ significantly whether moisturiser went on before or after sunscreen. Prescription products: follow your prescriber.

entries.title: Skincare routine basics (and Korean multi-step routines)
entries.answer: A short routine is what dermatologist guidance recommends: gentle cleanser, moisturiser and sunscreen. Scrubbing irritates and over-exfoliating is a common reason people see a dermatologist. I found no human study showing a long multi-step routine, Korean or otherwise, improves dark skin. Stop any product that burns or stings.

entries.title: Sleep, short sleep and sleep apnoea
entries.answer: In a US study Black adults were more likely to sleep under six hours and to have sleep apnoea than white adults, and most people with apnoea had never been told. Discrimination is also linked to shorter sleep. If you snore loudly, gasp or are always tired, see a GP. Regular habits help insomnia.

entries.title: Soursop (graviola): cancer cure, blood sugar and safety
entries.answer: There is no proof that soursop treats cancer; human studies are lacking. The fruit is eaten as food. In Guadeloupe, regular soursop consumption was closely linked to a rare, severe parkinsonism, with a plant chemical called annonacin as the probable cause. Do not use it instead of cancer treatment, and tell your doctor if you take it.

entries.title: Starting training, rest days and recovery
entries.answer: Nothing I found says Black adults need a different programme or rest days, so the NHS targets apply: strength work on two days, plus moderate or vigorous activity most days. One US survey found creatine kinase, a muscle blood marker, runs higher in Black adults, so a high result may be normal.

entries.title: Stigma, talking to family and starting therapy
entries.answer: A London study found stigma, silence and beliefs about causes slow help-seeking in African-descended communities, including in church groups. You can start without a diagnosis: in the UK you can refer yourself to NHS talking therapies for anxiety, depression and trauma. Telling one person you trust is a first step.

entries.title: Stress, burnout and blood pressure
entries.answer: Reported discrimination is linked to a higher chance of high blood pressure, but the link is small and not proven to be cause. Stress relief such as meditation may add to treatment, not replace it. If stress is wearing you down, talk to someone and get your blood pressure checked.

entries.title: Stretch marks and fading scars
entries.answer: No cream, butter or oil has been shown to stop stretch marks, and a trial of cocoa butter in pregnant women found it made no difference. They usually fade over time. Retinoid creams or hyaluronic acid may help new ones, and laser carries a higher risk of dark marks and burns in dark skin.

entries.title: Stroke: signs to act on and what raises the risk
entries.answer: A stroke is an emergency: a drooping face, a weak arm, slurred speech, then call emergency services at once, even if it passes. Black adults have strokes more often and younger in the studies we found, and high blood pressure is the biggest risk. Having your blood pressure checked and treated is the most useful step.

entries.title: Sunscreen on dark skin
entries.answer: Dark skin burns less easily and melanoma is rarer, but when it happens it is found later and survival is worse. In a small test on normal skin, visible light left darker, longer-lasting pigment than long-wave UVA. A broad-spectrum sunscreen is reasonable; whether sunscreen prevents melanoma in Black skin is untested.

entries.title: Sweat, body odour and deodorant
entries.answer: Sweating and odour are normal. I found nothing showing dark skin needs different handling. Antiperspirants, which reduce sweat, are the main tool; deodorants only mask smell. Loose, breathable clothing helps. If sweating is heavy, lasting, at night or running in your family, see a doctor.

entries.title: Taking too many vitamins and supplements
entries.answer: Yes. Food rarely causes trouble, but supplements can, and the safe daily ceiling differs by vitamin and by country. Some taken in large amounts cause stomach upset; others build up in the body, such as vitamin A and vitamin D. Add up everything you take, and ask a pharmacist or doctor if you are pregnant.

entries.title: Traction alopecia and 'protective' styles
entries.answer: Tight braids, weaves and ponytails can cause traction alopecia, hair loss from pulling, and the risk is highest when tension is added to relaxed hair. Caught early it can recover; left, it can become permanent. "Protective" describes the intention: tension is what matters.

entries.title: Turmeric and curcumin supplements
entries.answer: Turmeric and curcumin supplements may ease joint pain a little in low-quality trials, but NCCIH says we do not know enough to say they help. Our search found no trial of turmeric or curcumin in Black participants. Rare serious liver injury is reported, and some loose turmeric powder carries lead. Stop and see a doctor if you turn yellow.

entries.title: Twist-outs, braid-outs and wash-and-gos: technique
entries.answer: No study has tested how to set a twist-out, braid-out or wash-and-go, or how long one lasts. Creators and stylists give tips and they disagree, for example on starting on wet or stretched hair. The one dermatology point is to keep twists and braids loose at the scalp.

entries.title: Type 2 diabetes risk and blood sugar
entries.answer: In south London, people with Black African or Black Caribbean backgrounds had two to three times the risk of type 2 diabetes of White British people, and the gap was only partly explained by weight, blood pressure or deprivation. The NHS says check your risk from 25. Weight, activity and blood tests are where you act.

entries.title: Vitamin D and dark skin
entries.answer: Total vitamin D in the blood is lower in Black Americans, but so is the protein that carries it, and one study found the usable amount similar. Two trials in older Black American women found supplements did not slow bone loss. UK advice still says dark-skinned people should consider a daily supplement. They disagree.

entries.title: Vitamins and supplements: what the NHS says
entries.answer: The NHS says most people get all the nutrients they need from a varied, balanced diet. The main exception for you is vitamin D: people with African, African-Caribbean or South Asian backgrounds should consider a daily supplement all year. Do not take iron without a blood test, and tell a pharmacist about any herbal remedy if you take other medicines.

entries.title: Vitiligo
entries.answer: Vitiligo is loss of skin colour in patches, an autoimmune condition, not an infection. Patches are usually permanent, though treatment can bring back colour in some people: a prescription cream did in trials, with responses seen across skin types (not compared type by type). Pale patches burn more easily, so use sunscreen. Camouflage cream can cover them.

entries.title: Vitiligo, spread, starting age and treatment options
entries.answer: Vitiligo can start at any age, but a Cochrane review says more than half of people develop it before 20. It can spread over years, and nobody can predict how far. No treatment cures it. Light therapy and some prescription creams bring colour back in some people, slowly, and it can fade again.

entries.title: Wash day and routine for 4c hair
entries.answer: Nobody has tested a wash-day routine for tightly coiled hair. UK and US dermatologists give different intervals, from every week or two to every one to three weeks, so choose what keeps your scalp comfortable. They agree on conditioner every wash and gentle detangling. Which shampoo or leave-in is best is untested.

entries.title: Weight, BMI and losing weight safely
entries.answer: The NHS says people from Black African or African-Caribbean backgrounds are at risk of health problems at a slightly lower BMI: 23 to 27.4 is overweight and 27.5 or more is obese. Lose weight steadily, about half to one kilogram a week, with a balanced diet and activity. BMI cannot tell muscle from fat.

entries.title: Wigs, weaves and lace glue
entries.answer: No study has tested whether wigs protect your own hair. Dermatologists advise keeping your own hair clean and moisturised underneath, sewing in loosely, wearing a satin wig cap, and putting glue just in front of the hairline, not on it. Adhesives and synthetic hair can cause an itchy allergic rash, and removal can pull out edges.

entries.title: Winter care and shrinkage for coily hair
entries.answer: No study has tested winter care or shrinkage in coily hair. General dermatology advice for winter applies: keep hair moisturised, air dry when you can, limit heat, and space out chemical services. Shrinkage is simply how tightly coiled hair behaves; I found nothing saying it is a problem or a sign of health.
